question: In triangle ABC, angle A = 40°, side b = 7 cm (i.e., AC = 7 cm), and side a = 5 cm (i.e., BC = 5 cm). Use the sine formula to find all possible values of angle B. Explain why there are two possible values.
referenceAnswer: Using $\frac{b}{\sin B} = \frac{a}{\sin A}$: $\frac{7}{\sin B} = \frac{5}{\sin 40^\circ}$. Solving gives $\sin B = \frac{7 \sin 40^\circ}{5} \approx 0.900$, so $B \approx 64.1^\circ$ or $180^\circ - 64.1^\circ = 116^\circ$. Both are valid because $A + B < 180^\circ$ in each case.

question: In triangle ABC, angle A = 40°, side b = 7 cm, and side a = 10 cm. Show that only one value of angle B is possible, and find it correct to 3 significant figures.
referenceAnswer: Using $\frac{b}{\sin B} = \frac{a}{\sin A}$: $\frac{7}{\sin B} = \frac{10}{\sin 40^\circ}$. Then $\sin B = \frac{7 \sin 40^\circ}{10} \approx 0.450$, so $B \approx 26.7^\circ$. Since $A + B = 40^\circ + 26.7^\circ = 66.7^\circ < 180^\circ$, the obtuse supplement ($180^\circ - 26.7^\circ = 153.3^\circ$) would make $A + B > 180^\circ$, so it is invalid.

question: In triangle ABC, angle A = 120°, side b = 9 cm, and side a = 15 cm. Find angle B and angle C, and then find side c, all correct to 3 significant figures.
referenceAnswer: Using $\frac{b}{\sin B} = \frac{a}{\sin A}$: $\frac{9}{\sin B} = \frac{15}{\sin 120^\circ}$. So $\sin B = \frac{9 \sin 120^\circ}{15} \approx 0.520$, giving $B \approx 31.3^\circ$. Then $C = 180^\circ - 120^\circ - 31.3^\circ = 28.7^\circ$. Using $\frac{c}{\sin C} = \frac{a}{\sin A}$: $c = \frac{15 \sin 28.7^\circ}{\sin 120^\circ} \approx 8.32$ cm.

question: In triangle ABC, angle A = 120°, side b = 9 cm, and side a = $5\sqrt{3}$ cm. Explain why no triangle can be formed with these measurements.
referenceAnswer: Using $\frac{b}{\sin B} = \frac{a}{\sin A}$: $\frac{9}{\sin B} = \frac{5\sqrt{3}}{\sin 120^\circ}$. Since $\sin 120^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, this gives $\sin B = \frac{9 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}{5\sqrt{3}} = \frac{9}{10} = 0.9$, so $B \approx 64.2^\circ$. But then $A + B = 120^\circ + 64.2^\circ = 184.2^\circ > 180^\circ$, violating the angle sum property — so no triangle exists.
evidence: Supplementary Example 5(b): '$\frac{9}{\sin B} = \frac{5\sqrt{3}}{\sin 120^\circ}$; $B = 64.2^\circ$; $A + B = 184.2^\circ > 180^\circ$; $\therefore$ No solution'

question: In triangle ABC, angle B = 30° and side AB = 20 cm. Kelvin says the shortest possible length of side AC is 10 cm. Verify his claim using trigonometry and explain why this is the minimum.
referenceAnswer: Side AC is opposite angle B. By the definition of sine in right triangle context (or by considering altitude from A to BC), the shortest AC occurs when triangle ABC is right-angled at C, so $\sin 30^\circ = \frac{AC}{AB} = \frac{AC}{20}$. Then $AC = 20 \sin 30^\circ = 20 \times 0.5 = 10$ cm. For any other position of C, AC is longer — so 10 cm is indeed the minimum.
